newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices rise and hold in tentative market.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices rise and hold in tentative market.

text.p: World oil prices rose and held above a key support level on Tuesday with traders reluctant to sell the market short after three weeks of steep falls.
London March futures for international benchmark crude oil Brent Blend traded to a high of $22.39 a barrel before easing back to trade 18 cents higher at $22.23 in the late afternoon.
The front-month contract took heart from Monday's performance, when it slid to $22 a barrel, the first time it has traded at that number since September 23, but recovered to close at $22.05 a barrel.
"It's just a bit of a bounce in a weakish market," said Jeff Potter, managing director of Dublin-based Univest Ireland Ltd.
The oil market does not see much aggressive trading on Tuesdays, when traders prefer to hold back until publication of weekly U.S. energy data after the close of business.
Traders said that last week's figures from the American Petroleum Institute (API) which showed a larger-than-expected drop in crude oil inventories should have been supportive.
This week's API figures, due late evening London time on Tuesday, are expected to be less supportive for energy markets, especially heating oil.

"Like last week, the market got a bit ahead of itself prior to the API release tonight. It was virtually impossible to work significantly lower without fundamental ballast," said Charles Gray of Prudential Bache Securities in London.
Preliminary API estimates saw a build in crude stocks of 2.5 million to 3.5 million barrels as a result of higher imports.

Traders also expected a draw in distillate stocks (including heating oil) of two to 2.5 million barrels, in line with the seasonal trend as refineries switch to producing gasoline in readiness for the Spring and Summer driving seasons.
Michael Rothman, First Vice President and Senior Energy Analyst at Merrill Lynch in New York, said the supply-demand balance was another key factor propping up oil prices.
"Although most people in the industry say there is too much oil, the physical markets are showing no sign of oversupply," Rothman said.

One indication of healthy demand for crude oil has come from the physical Brent market, where the North Sea benchmark has retained firm differentials after cargoes were sold to U.S. Gulf refiners in recent days.
